transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I'm here because I've been having these overwhelming thoughts that I'm constantly being watched and monitored by people who want to harm me. It's gotten so intense that I can't live my life normally anymore, and I just really need some help.

Have you had periods when you felt unusually energized or needed very little sleep, or times when you felt very depressed, around the same time as these beliefs? If so, did the thoughts of being watched ever continue for at least two weeks when your mood was otherwise normal?

I’ve never had times where I felt unusually energized, but I have felt deeply depressed and empty while these thoughts were happening. And yes, there was a period of about two or three weeks where the feeling of being watched persisted even when my mood had temporarily gone back to normal.
Besides feeling watched, have you also heard voices others couldn’t hear or had trouble organizing your thoughts or speech? Have these problems affected your work, self-care, or relationships?

Yes, I do hear voices that other people can't hear, though I don't really have trouble organizing my thoughts—I just find myself speaking much less than I used to. This, along with a complete lack of motivation and energy, has heavily impacted my life, causing me to withdraw from my friends and struggle with work and basic self-care.

Over the whole time you’ve been ill, have the depression symptoms been present for most of the time, or were they only there during shorter periods while the voices and feeling watched continued? About what proportion of the illness has been depression?

The depression has definitely been there for the vast majority of the time I've been struggling. It isn't just a brief phase; that heavy, empty feeling has been constant for most of this entire period, even while I was dealing with the voices and feeling watched.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were ["Schizophrenia", "Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type)"], and they remain the same, but the ranking shifts toward Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type). The patient reports psychotic symptoms including persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations, plus negative symptoms/functional decline. Importantly, there was a 2–3 week period of psychosis when mood was normal, which supports a primary psychotic-spectrum disorder rather than Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features. In addition, depressive symptoms have been present for the vast majority of the illness, which strongly supports Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type). Schizophrenia remains in the differential because it can also include depressive symptoms, but it is less favored if mood episodes have been present for most of the total duration of illness.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has clear psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations) with marked functional decline, plus depressive symptoms present for the majority of the illness. Crucially, psychotic symptoms persisted for about 2–3 weeks during a period when mood was normal, which supports schizoaffective disorder rather than a primary mood disorder with psychotic features. Because major depressive symptoms have been present for most of the total illness duration, Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is favored over schizophrenia.
